Subsist means to continue to exist or stay alive, but almost always with the underlying suggestion of barely, minimally, or with great difficulty. It is the word you reach for when someone or something is surviving, but only at the most basic, stripped-down level — not thriving, not comfortable, just... managing to keep going.

Think of it as the verb that lives right on the edge between "alive" and "not alive," between "existing" and "disappearing."

Sense 1 — To survive on the bare minimum (most common use)

This is how you will encounter the word most of the time. When a person or group subsists, they are keeping themselves alive or functioning using only the most minimal resources — usually food, money, or basic necessities. The word almost always signals hardship, scarcity, or severe limitation.

The key feeling here is: just enough, and nothing more.

"The prisoners subsisted on a single bowl of broth per day."
"During the drought, the villagers subsisted on whatever roots and berries they could find."
"He lost his job and spent months subsisting on savings."

Notice that in this sense, "subsist" almost always pairs with "on" or "by":

  • subsist on (a resource) → subsist on rice, subsist on $10 a day
  • subsist by (doing something) → subsist by fishing, subsist by selling small goods

Sense 2 — To continue to exist (more formal use)

In a broader, more formal sense, subsist simply means to persist or to remain in existence — often used for traditions, ideas, institutions, or conditions that haven't disappeared yet, even though they perhaps should have, or even though most things around them have changed.

"A few ancient tribal customs still subsist in that remote region."
"The old rivalry between the two families continued to subsist for generations."
"Poverty subsists even in the wealthiest nations."

Here there's no food or money involved — the word is just saying: this thing has not died out; it is still here.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is important, because words carry emotional weight beyond their dictionary meaning.

Subsist is never a cheerful word. Even in its neutral, formal sense (Sense 2), it carries a quiet shadow — a suggestion that whatever is existing is doing so in a diminished or precarious way. When you say something subsists, you are subtly signaling that its existence is fragile, minimal, or in some way insufficient.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The family lived on a farm." — neutral, no judgment
  • "The family subsisted on a farm." — immediately suggests struggle, hardship, scarcity

The second sentence, just by using "subsisted," tells you that life was hard. That is the power of this word.
How It Is Different from Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing where its edges are — where it ends and another word begins.

Subsist vs. Survive — These are close, but survive simply means to make it through something (often a specific event or danger). Subsist is more about ongoing, day-to-day minimal existence. You survive a crash; you subsist on little food over many years.

Subsist vs. Thrive — These are near opposites. Thrive means to flourish and grow strongly. Subsist means to barely hold on. A plant that thrives is lush and growing; a plant that subsists is alive but stunted.

Subsist vs. Exist — Exist is completely neutral. A rock exists. A cloud exists. But subsist always carries that added layer: existing with difficulty, or in a diminished state. You would never say "a rock subsists." It implies some kind of struggle or precariousness.

Subsist vs. Sustain — Easy to confuse, but different roles. Sustain is usually something you do to something else (you sustain a person; food sustains you). Subsist is something you do by yourself, often on something else (you subsist on food). Also, "sustain" has no suggestion of scarcity; "subsist" almost always does.
Putting It All Together — A Mental Picture

Imagine a person stranded on a deserted island. They are not eating well, not comfortable, not flourishing — but they are alive. They have found a small stream to drink from and catch one or two small fish each day. They are getting by. They are making it. Just barely.

That person is subsisting.

Now imagine that same person ten years later — the island has been discovered, they have built a shelter, they have crops, they are no longer in danger. Now you would not use "subsist." Now they are living, perhaps even thriving.

The moment between near-death and genuine living — that narrow, difficult space — is where "subsist" lives.

• "Millions of people in the region subsist on less than two dollars a day." (surviving on barely enough money)
  • "The monks subsisted on bread, water, and prayer." (minimal food, austere life)
  • "After the factory closed, she subsisted by doing odd jobs." (getting by through whatever means possible)
  • "Pockets of the old language still subsist in highland communities." (continuing to exist, not yet gone)
  • "The tradition of handmade pottery subsists despite the rise of mass production." (persisting against the odds)

That is the full picture of subsist — a word about barely-enough existence, quiet endurance, and the fragile persistence of things that are alive but struggling.
